Notes: Year Established -650 = 7th c. BCE midpoint: per B. Mazar (Encyclopaedia Judaica) the Judahite town on Tel Goren (Stratum V, a royal estate producing balsam) was established only in the 7th century BCE; this is the earliest documented Judahite presence. EVENT: this first settlement was apparently destroyed and burned by Nebuchadnezzar in 582/1 BCE (c.). No statement that no Jews remained, so Population blank.

Persian period (5th-4th c. BCE; midpoint convention -435): Stratum IV on Tel Goren, a town more extensive than the Israelite one with larger well-built buildings; many sherds inscribed 'Yehud' show En-Gedi belonged to the province of Judah. Presence of a Judean (Yehud) settlement; no population figure (B. Mazar, Encyclopaedia Judaica).

Persian period (midpoint convention): review by A. Nunn (Abstracta Iranica 30, 2010) of S. Matskevich & E. Stern, 'Stratum IV - The Persian Period', En-Gedi Excavations I. Final Report (1961-1965), IEJ 2007, pp. 193-270: architecture is a large residence of c. 30 x 30 m; local coarse pottery, much Attic black-glaze and figured ware; a few Yehud-type stamp impressions, lion stamps; two Neo-Babylonian seals in Achaemenid layers. Yehud impressions indicate a Judean provincial settlement; no population figure. (Text extracted locally from PDF.)

c. 4th c. BCE (midpoint -350): BibleWalks (citing Mazar excavations and NEAEHL) states the Persian-period village, repopulated after the return from exile, 'continued until the 4th century, then was deserted'. Recorded as a documented abandonment (0); exact date unknown and the source is a popular site, so treat with caution. Resettlement followed under the Hasmoneans.

Hasmonean period (140-37 BCE convention -90): BibleWalks states the Hasmonean kings, starting from John Hyrcanus I (134-104 BCE) and especially Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE), rebuilt the oasis, marking the rise of a new Ein Gedi; a fortress on Tel Goren dated from Jannaeus until Herod. Event: Hasmonean re-founding of a Judean settlement; no figure.

Stratum III belongs to the Hasmonean period; En-Gedi flourished especially under Alexander Jannaeus and his successors (103-37 BCE; midpoint -70). A large fortress on the tell was probably destroyed during the Parthian invasion / Hasmonean-Herodian conflict (B. Mazar, Encyclopaedia Judaica). Presence of a flourishing Judean settlement; no figure.

Late Hasmonean period (c.; -70 as midpoint of 103-37 BCE): Wikipedia, citing G. Hadas 1994 ('Nine Tombs of the Second Temple Period at En Gedi', Atiqot 24), says Ein Gedi was likely inhabited by tenant farmers who reused cave tombs for multiple burials; several well-preserved wooden coffins of the 2nd-1st c. BCE. Jewish village presence; tenant-farmer/royal-estate interpretation is contested (no literary source supports it). No figure.

EVENT c. 40-37 BCE: the Hasmonean fortress on Tel Goren (c. 3,500 sq m) was destroyed during the Parthian conquest (40-37 BCE) or during the battles with Herod (BibleWalks, citing NEAEHL). No statement on residents.

EVENT c. 40 BCE: S. Goranson (Orion Center symposium 1998) argues that Pliny NH 5.73 ('Engada ... nunc alterum bustum', now another ash-heap) drew on M. Vipsanius Agrippa, who referred to the destruction of Ein Gedi c. 40 BCE during the Parthian invasion and Jewish civil war, not the First Revolt. Scholarly interpretation; other scholars (Cotton) link the passage to 68 CE.

c. 40-37 BCE: Y. Farhi 2022 (Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology 3) publishes a bronze finger ring found in a burial cave in the Nahal David cliff at En Gedi (excavated by N. Avigad) bearing a symbol known mainly from coins of Mattathias Antigonus; he links the cave's burials to the conflict between Herod and Antigonus (40-37 BCE). Evidence of Judean burials of the period; no figure.

34 BCE: H. M. Cotton (SCI 20, 2001) - En-Gedi and its balsam groves were part of the royal domain under the Hasmonean and Herodian dynasties (Pliny NH 12.111: balsam in two royal gardens, Jericho and Ein Gedi); in 34 BCE Mark Antony gave the balsam (with the dates of Jericho) to Cleopatra, from whom Herod leased them; Herodian rule ended with Archelaus' exile in 6 CE. Event affecting the settlement's status; no population figure. (Text extracted locally from PDF.)

Herodian period (37-4 BCE convention -20): Wikipedia, citing Y. Porath 2021 (The Synagogue at En-Gedi, Qedem 64), states Ein Gedi reached its greatest extent in the Herodian period, the settlement spreading north of Tel Goren across the natural terrace. Expansion of the Jewish village; no figure given for this period (the c. 1,000 estimate cited on the page is Byzantine).

Herodian (convention -20): Hirschfeld's excavation (NEAEHL) found a well-preserved square miqveh (ritual bath; 1.7 x 1.7 m, 1.7 m deep) plastered with grey hydraulic plaster characteristic of the Herodian period; vessels on its floor under a burn layer linked by the excavator to the Sicarii massacre of spring 68 CE. Domestic Jewish ritual-purity installation; no figure.

Early Roman period (63 BCE-70 CE convention 4): Early Roman stratum of the village (Hirschfeld, NEAEHL) yielded pottery, painted Nabatean bowls and coins of Alexander Jannaeus, Herod, Agrippa I and the procurators - domestic occupation of the Jewish village through the Hasmonean-Herodian-procuratorial periods; no figure.

1st c. BCE-1st c. CE (midpoint; no year 0, so 1 used): some 40 wooden coffins found in family burial tombs at En-Gedi in G. Hadas's 1984-1988 surveys/excavations; pottery in the burial caves dates the coffins from the 1st c. BCE to the 1st c. CE (NEAEHL). Family tombs of the Jewish village; suggests an established resident community; no figure.

1st-early 2nd c. CE (midpoint 1st c. CE = 50): Archaeology magazine (1999) reports Y. Hirschfeld's excavation of 28 one-person dwellings on the edge of the oasis above Ein Gedi, occupied in the 1st and early 2nd c. CE (and again 4th-6th c.), possibly an Essene community whose members worked the oasis fields. A sect subset (c. 28 single-person cells), not the town's population, so Population blank; the Essene identification is widely contested (others see seasonal shelters/storage sheds).

c. 66 CE: Josephus, War 3.3.5 (3.54-55) lists Engaddi among the eleven toparchies of Judea ('and Idumea, and Engaddi, and Herodium, and Jericho'), i.e. Ein Gedi was the head village of a Judean district on the eve of the revolt. Primary text; no figure.

Second year of the First Revolt (67/68 CE): a residential quarter west/north-west of the synagogue excavated 2003-2005, with a single occupation level, was destroyed in the second year of the First Jewish Revolt (NEAEHL). Evidence of a Second Temple-period suburb of the Jewish village and its destruction; no figure.

EVENT Passover 68 CE: Josephus, War 4.7.2 (4.402-405): the Sicarii from Masada overran 'a certain small city called Engaddi', drove off the men, and 'as for such as could not run away, being women and children, they slew of them above seven hundred', then plundered the houses and carried off the crops to Masada. Ancient casualty figure (700+ women and children killed) - a death toll, not a population count, so Population blank; it implies a town of at least several hundred to over a thousand residents.

EVENT 68 CE: Stratum II, a fortress on the tell attributed to Herod's successors (4 BCE-68 CE), was destroyed during the Jewish War in 68 CE; coins from 'Year Two' of the revolt were found in the conflagration area. Josephus describes En-Gedi as the capital of a Judean toparchy and records its destruction in the war (B. Mazar, Encyclopaedia Judaica).

EVENT 68 CE: H. M. Cotton (SCI 20, 2001): after the Sicarii raid at Passover 68 (Josephus War 4.402-4) and the battles between Jews and the Roman army over the balsam groves when Vespasian was at Jericho (June 68), Ein Gedi 'must have been practically abandoned, at least for a while'; Jewish families who escaped settled at Mahoz Eglatain (Mahoza) in the Nabataean kingdom. Cotton reads Pliny NH 5.73 ('now, like Jerusalem, a heap of ashes') as describing this ruin. 'Practically abandoned' is not stated as total, so Population blank. (Text extracted locally from PDF.)

c. 68 CE (revolt dated 66-70 CE by the source; destruction of Ein Gedi in 68): Jewish Virtual Library (Israel MFA text) states that after thriving in the Hasmonean-Herodian periods as a royal estate with a fortified citadel, 'Ein Gedi was destroyed and abandoned during the First Jewish Rebellion against Rome (66-70 CE)'. Documented abandonment = 0. The village was resettled between the revolts (Roman bath, coins; Jewish residents attested by 124 CE).
